action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open, in their organization.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: One or two emoji for the browser-tab icon (e.g. "📊"), with no markup. Required on a page's first publish. On a redeploy Claude omits it so the artifact keeps its icon, and passes a new one only when the person asks. Optional with `type_url` and for a typed Artifact's data files.

icon.description: Optional. One short generic word for the artifact's tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map — a plain signifier, not a product or brand name. Omit when republishing to keep the current icon. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open in the same organization, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact and it must be in your organization.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to types whose title or description contains this text, ignoring case. Omitting it lists them all.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, which must be one the person owns; Claude omits it for a new artifact or a redeploy in the same conversation (see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**). For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

content.content:
# Link — the arrow that says why

## Purpose

A link is one causal claim: *this proposition makes that proposition more (or less) likely, and here is the mechanism*. Before links, a user could say "Hormuz opening is bullish for oil" and be believed or not. With links, every step of that story is a separate arrow carrying a sentence of mechanism, a signed number for how hard it pushes, a delay for when the push arrives, a shape for what it looks like over time, and a record of where the number came from. The user can click any arrow, read the reason, disagree with the number, and watch what that does downstream. Nothing on the canvas is an opinion without a stated reason — which is the whole product.

---

## Data model

Two frozen shapes, written as pydantic models — pydantic being the Python library we use to define a data shape and check anything claiming to be one. *Frozen* means an instance can never be changed after it is built; a change is a new instance, recorded as an intervention on a branch (see [`../multiverse/interventions.md`](../multiverse/interventions.md)).

**A warning about the word *source*.** It does four different jobs in this part of the spec. `Link.source` is the **cause**, the claim an arrow starts at. `Link.sources` is the **citations** backing that arrow. `Source` is the type of one of those citations. And `Resolution.source` in [`proposition.md`](proposition.md) is the **adjudicator**, whoever decides if a claim came true. Where this chapter means the first it says *cause*; where it means the second or third it says *source* or *citation*; the fourth never appears here.

```python
from datetime import date
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

from katalyst.domain.proposition import PropositionId  # a plain `str`; defined in `proposition.md`

LinkId = str

Days = float
"""A span of time measured in days. 1.0 is one day, 0.5 is twelve hours, 14.0 is
a fortnight. A plain number rather than a duration written as text (the style
that writes a fortnight as "P14D"), because such a duration crosses to the
browser as a string, and nobody can do timing arithmetic on a string."""

Provenance = Literal[
    "asserted", "argued", "documented", "market_implied", "user", "historical", "simulated"
]
"""Where a number or a link came from. Set by our pipeline from what actually
happened, never declared by the model. The seven values are defined in the
table below and in `../vocabulary.md`."""


class Source(BaseModel):
    """Something a reader can open to check what we are claiming.

    A source exists because our retrieval step actually fetched a document, or
    because a person typed one in. It is never something the model reports
    having read. A `Source` is never invented to make a link look
    better than it is.
    """

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    url: str = Field(
        description="Where the reader goes to check it. One address that opens, not a search query."
    )
    title: str = Field(
        description="What the reader will see when they get there, in the publisher's words, not ours."
    )
    retrieved: date | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description="The day our retrieval step fetched it. None when a person supplied the source by hand.",
    )


class Link(BaseModel):
    """A causal claim from one proposition to another: A makes B more, or less, likely.

    A link is an argument, not a correlation. It must say why it thinks the
    mechanism is real (`rationale`), how hard it pushes (`strength`), how long
    the push takes to arrive (`lag`), what the push looks like over time
    (`shape`), and whether the push survives its cause going away (`mode`).

    A link must never carry a number without a reason. A link with no
    rationale, or one claiming evidence it does not cite, is rejected with a
    message — never quietly patched up. See `validity.md`.
    """

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    id: LinkId = Field(
        description="Minted by our code, never by the model. See `validity.md`, section Identifiers."
    )
    source: PropositionId = Field(
        description="The cause. The proposition this arrow starts at. Must name a proposition in the same graph."
    )
    target: PropositionId = Field(
        description="The effect. The proposition this arrow ends at. Must name a proposition in the same graph."
    )

    mode: Literal["trigger", "sustain"] = Field(
        description=(
            "How the push behaves when the cause goes away. 'trigger': a one-time shove — once the "
            "cause becomes true the effect is pushed and stays pushed, fading on its own; undoing the "
            "cause later does not undo it (a toppled domino). 'sustain': a continuous hold — the push "
            "exists only while the cause holds, and vanishes the moment it stops (a desk under an apple)."
        )
    )
    strength: float = Field(
        description=(
            "How far this link shifts the target's log-odds while the push is at full size. Signed: "
            "positive makes the target claim more likely to be TRUE, negative less likely. This is not a "
            "probability and is not capped at 1. Roughly: +1 triples the odds, -1 cuts them to a third."
        )
    )
    lag: Days = Field(
        description=(
            "Days from the cause becoming true to the push reaching full size. 0.0 means the same day. "
            "Must be greater than 0 when `reflexive` is true (INV-6)."
        )
    )
    shape: Literal["impulse", "step", "ramp"] = Field(
        description=(
            "What the push does over time. 'impulse': nothing during the lag, then a spike that decays "
            "by `half_life`. 'step': nothing during the lag, then full size, held. 'ramp': climbs from "
            "nothing to full size across the lag, then held."
        )
    )
    half_life: Days | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description=(
            "Days for an 'impulse' push to fall to half its size. Meaningful only when `shape` is "
            "'impulse'; None for 'step' and 'ramp'."
        ),
    )

    rationale: str = Field(
        description=(
            "The mechanism in one to three plain sentences: why this cause moves this effect. Required "
            "on every link. An empty rationale is a violation, not a default (INV-2)."
        )
    )
    sources: tuple[Source, ...] = Field(
        default=(),
        description=(

            "'documented', 'historical' or 'market_implied' (INV-2)."
        ),
    )

        description=(
            "Where this link and its number came from, as a fact about our pipeline. Set by `engine/` "
            "from what actually happened; the model never fills this in (decision record 0003, rule 5)."
        )
    )
    reflexive: bool = Field(
        default=False,
        description=(
            "True when this arrow is a market feeding back on the world — a price outcome changing what "
            "people do. A reflexive link is allowed to close a loop, and must have `lag > 0` (INV-6)."

### Strength, and what log-odds means

The **odds** of a claim are the chance it is true divided by the chance it is false: a 50% claim is 1-to-1 odds, a 75% claim is 3-to-1. **Log-odds** is the natural logarithm of that ratio, and it is the scale on which independent pushes *add* instead of multiplying — so a proposition with three parents gets three numbers added together, not a table of every combination. | `strength` | a 50% claim becomes | in words |
|---:|---:|---|
| −3.0 | 5% | close to ruled out |
| −2.0 | 12% | a strong push against |
| −1.0 | 27% | a clear push against |
| −0.5 | 38% | a nudge against |
| 0.0 | 50% | no effect — never draw this link |
| +0.5 | 62% | a nudge toward |
| +1.0 | 73% | a clear push toward |
| +2.0 | 88% | a strong push toward |
| +3.0 | 95% | close to decisive |

The push is relative, not absolute. The same +1.0 applied to a claim we thought was 5% likely takes it to about 13%, not to 73%. That is the property we want: no sum of pushes can ever drive a probability below 0 or above 1.

**The sign is on the claim, not on the world.** `strength` is positive when the cause makes the *target proposition come out TRUE* more often. A proposition reading "Brent crude settles below $68" is made **more** likely by the strait opening, so that arrow is **positive** — even though the thing it describes is the oil price going *down*. Research report 02 writes that arrow as −1.6; it was thinking about the price, not about the claim. The claim wins.

### The two modes: the domino and the apple

This is Kent's idea from `docs/initial-brainstorming.md`, and research report 02 §4 called it the best one in the notes. In his words: two things can depend on each other *sequentially* — toppling dominoes, where "an earlier domino can be reset without changing the overall effect of the chain of dominoes being toppled" — or one can require *the sustained existence* of the other, like an apple sitting on a desk, held up only as long as the desk keeps pushing back against gravity.

| | `trigger` — the domino | `sustain` — the apple on the desk |
|---|---|---|
| When it pushes | Once, when the cause becomes true | Continuously, for as long as the cause holds |
| If the cause is undone later | Nothing happens. The effect stays pushed and keeps fading on its own | The push is withdrawn. The effect retracts |
| Typical shape | `impulse`, sometimes `ramp` | `step` |
| Hormuz example | The war-risk premium priced into crude unwinds once, over weeks | Insurers keep the premium low only while the lane stays open |
| The plain sentence | "It already happened" | "It is still happening" |

```

                   │                       │
trigger (domino)   ▼                       ▼
push on effect ────█████▇▇▆▆▅▅▄▄▃▃▂▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁

                     t1 changes nothing — the domino stays fallen.

sustain (apple on desk)
push on effect ────████████████████████████▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁
                   └ holds while the cause holds …

# Link — the arrow that says why

## Purpose

A link is one causal claim: *this proposition makes that proposition more (or less) likely, and here is the mechanism*. Before links, a user could say "Hormuz opening is bullish for oil" and be believed or not. With links, every step of that story is a separate arrow carrying a sentence of mechanism, a signed number for how hard it pushes, a delay for when the push arrives, a shape for what it looks like over time, and a record of where the number came from. The user can click any arrow, read the reason, disagree with the number, and watch what that does downstream. Nothing on the canvas is an opinion without a stated reason — which is the whole product.

---

Two frozen shapes, written as pydantic models — pydantic being the Python library we use to define a data shape and check anything claiming to be one. *Frozen* means an instance can never be changed after it is built; a change is a new instance, recorded as an intervention on a branch (see [`../multiverse/interventions.md`](../multiverse/interventions.md)).

**A warning about the word *source*.** It does four different jobs in this part of the spec. `Link.source` is the **cause**, the claim an arrow starts at. `Link.sources` is the **citations** backing that arrow. `Source` is the type of one of those citations. And `Resolution.source` in [`proposition.md`](proposition.md) is the **adjudicator**, whoever decides if a claim came true. Where this chapter means the first it says *cause*; where it means the second or third it says *source* or *citation*; the fourth never appears here.

LinkId = str

"""A span of time measured in days. 1.0 is one day, 0.5 is twelve hours, 14.0 is
a fortnight. A plain number rather than a duration written as text (the style
that writes a fortnight as "P14D"), because such a duration crosses to the
browser as a string, and nobody can do timing arithmetic on a string."""

Provenance = Literal[
    "asserted", "argued", "documented", "market_implied", "user", "historical", "simulated"
]
"""Where a number or a link came from. Set by our pipeline from what actually
happened, never declared by the model. The seven values are defined in the
table below and in `../vocabulary.md`."""


class Source(BaseModel):
    """Something a reader can open to check what we are claiming.

    A source exists because our retrieval step actually fetched a document, or
    because a person typed one in. It is never something the model reports
    having read. A `Source` is never invented to make a link look
    better than it is.
    """

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    url: str = Field(
        description="Where the reader goes to check it. One address that opens, not a search query."
    )
    title: str = Field(
        description="What the reader will see when they get there, in the publisher's words, not ours."
    )
    retrieved: date | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description="The day our retrieval step fetched it. None when a person supplied the source by hand.",
    )


class Link(BaseModel):
    """A causal claim from one proposition to another: A makes B more, or less, likely.

    A link is an argument, not a correlation. It must say why it thinks the
    mechanism is real (`rationale`), how hard it pushes (`strength`), how long
    the push takes to arrive (`lag`), what the push looks like over time
    (`shape`), and whether the push survives its cause going away (`mode`).

    A link must never carry a number without a reason. A link with no
    rationale, or one claiming evidence it does not cite, is rejected with a
    message — never quietly patched up. See `validity.md`.
    """

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    id: LinkId = Field(
        description="Minted by our code, never by the model. See `validity.md`, section Identifiers."
    )
    source: PropositionId = Field(
        description="The cause. The proposition this arrow starts at. Must name a proposition in the same graph."
    )
    target: PropositionId = Field(
        description="The effect. The proposition this arrow ends at. Must name a proposition in the same graph."
    )

    mode: Literal["trigger", "sustain"] = Field(
        description=(
            "How the push behaves when the cause goes away. 'trigger': a one-time shove — once the "
            "cause becomes true the effect is pushed and stays pushed, fading on its own; undoing the "
            "cause later does not undo it (a toppled domino). 'sustain': a continuous hold — the push "
            "exists only while the cause holds, and vanishes the moment it stops (a desk under an apple)."
        )
    )
    strength: float = Field(
        description=(
            "How far this link shifts the target's log-odds while the push is at full size. Signed: "
            "positive makes the target claim more likely to be TRUE, negative less likely. This is not a "
            "probability and is not capped at 1. Roughly: +1 triples the odds, -1 cuts them to a third."
        )
    )
    lag: Days = Field(
        description=(
            "Days from the cause becoming true to the push reaching full size. 0.0 means the same day. "
            "Must be greater than 0 when `reflexive` is true (INV-6)."
        )
    )
    shape: Literal["impulse", "step", "ramp"] = Field(
        description=(
            "What the push does over time. 'impulse': nothing during the lag, then a spike that decays "
            "by `half_life`. 'step': nothing during the lag, then full size, held. 'ramp': climbs from "
            "nothing to full size across the lag, then held."
        )
    )
    half_life: Days | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description=(
            "Days for an 'impulse' push to fall to half its size. Meaningful only when `shape` is "
            "'impulse'; None for 'step' and 'ramp'."
        ),
    )

    rationale: str = Field(
        description=(
            "The mechanism in one to three plain sentences: why this cause moves this effect. Required "
            "on every link. An empty rationale is a violation, not a default (INV-2)."
        )
    )
    sources: tuple[Source, ...] = Field(
        default=(),
        description=(
            "What backs the link. At least one is required when `provenance` claims evidence — "
            "'documented', 'historical' or 'market_implied' (INV-2)."
        ),
    )
    provenance: Provenance = Field(
        description=(
            "Where this link and its number came from, as a fact about our pipeline. Set by `engine/` "
            "from what actually happened; the model never fills this in (decision record 0003, rule 5)."
        )
    )
    reflexive: bool = Field(
        default=False,
        description=(
            "True when this arrow is a market feeding back on the world — a price outcome changing what "
            "people do. A reflexive link is allowed to close a loop, and must have `lag > 0` (INV-6)."
        ),
    )

# Stack 03a — the engine

**Waiting on Kent** (decisions this plan had to take because nobody had; each is marked *decided here* in the pre-decisions table and each is cheap to reverse): **(1)** how a supposition *ends* — a "suppose this is true" is overridden from the day a later arrow pushes against it, and the claim falls back to its own baseline plus every live arrow; **(2)** `lo`–`hi` on a computed belief means the 10th-to-90th-percentile band across parameter draws; **(3)** `ramp` keeps using `lag` as its rise time — no new `rise_time` field; **(4)** `strength` gets no hard ceiling, only a warning above ±5; **(5)** a `half_life` on a `step` or `ramp` arrow is ignored with a warning, not a new violation code; **(6)** the day the map starts from (`as_of`) is passed into `propagate` — `Graph` grows no date field; **(7)** a claim nothing has asserted and nothing is pushing turns true on day zero; **(8)** a claim's headline number is read on its own resolve-by day; **(9)** the delta rail's ranking formula (size × how well-founded); **(10)** ten thousand draws by default, two thousand for the sensitivity sweep.

---

**Goal:** change one step and only what is downstream moves — and the change is a number you can watch travel. After this stack, the Hormuz map plus the strike branch produces two worlds, a difference between them, and a ranked list of what moved, all from three inputs: a base map, a branch, and a seed.

**What this stack must not do.** No model. No network. No interface. Nothing under `frontend/` except the one generated types file. No persistence. No thesis card, no stop-loss, no market prices. `refine` stays a type with no behaviour (stack 06). Reflexive arrows stay data: the loop check already sets them aside and this stack does not unroll them (stack 06).

**Rests on:** decision record 0004 (a branch is an ordered list of edits over an untouched base), 0005 (what a link carries and how likelihoods flow: log-odds addition, trigger and sustain, seeded random simulation), 0008 (the test names). Read all three "Decision Outcome" sections before writing anything. The two chapters merged in stack 02 — `spec/multiverse/interventions.md` and `spec/multiverse/branches-and-worlds.md` — are the contract this stack implements; their INVARIANTS sections already name every test below and tag them **stack 03a**.

## Pull request 2 — `apply`

### The shapes

```python
class Assignment(BaseModel):          # frozen, like everything in domain/
    target: PropositionId             # the claim an edit fixed
    value: bool                       # what it was fixed to
    at: date | None                   # the day it holds from; None means day zero
    by: int                           # which edit did it: its position in the branch, counting from 0
    kind: Literal["do", "observe"]    # which of the two verbs the user chose
```

```python
def apply(
    graph: Graph,
    branch: Branch,
    assignments: tuple[Assignment, ...] = (),
) -> tuple[Graph, tuple[Assignment, ...]] | list[Violation]
```

`apply` folds a branch's edits onto a map, in order, and hands back the map it leaves behind together with every value an edit fixed. It is pure: no clock, no network, no randomness. The optional third argument is what makes law 2 type-check — feed back what a previous `apply` returned and you can apply the next branch on top:

```
apply(g, x + y)  ==  apply(g2, y, a2)   where (g2, a2) = apply(g, x)
```

**What each edit does to the map.** `do`: remove every arrow whose target is this claim **and that is present right now** — a timed assertion, not a seal — and record an assignment. `observe`: remove nothing; record an assignment. `insert`: add the claim and its arrows. `retune`: replace one arrow's `strength` and nothing else. `believe`: write `beliefs.user` on one claim and nothing else, anywhere. `refine`: **not implemented** — return a violation saying it arrives in stack 06.

**Failure is a list of violations, never an exception and never a half-applied branch.** Three new codes join the twelve in `domain/validity.py`, exactly the three `interventions.md` open question 5 proposed: `unknown_target` (the edit names a claim this map does not have), `unknown_link` (it names an arrow this map does not have), `duplicate_id` (an `insert` reuses an identifier). Their messages are interface text — a plain sentence naming the claim or arrow by its words, not by its identifier, like every message already in `validity.py`.

**`flatten`.** A child branch applies its parent's edits first, and `domain/` sees one branch at a time, never the collection. So `flatten(branches: Mapping[BranchId, Branch], branch_id: BranchId) -> tuple[Intervention, ...]` walks the parent chain and concatenates. A parent chain that loops back on itself returns a violation rather than hanging (`branches-and-worlds.md` open question 3, answered here for the walk only — the storage rule is still stack 05's).

**`affected_set(graph, intervention) -> frozenset[PropositionId]`** computes, from the shape of the map alone using `networkx`, the claims an edit is allowed to move. One branch per row of the affected-set table in `interventions.md` §INVARIANTS. Read that table as the specification; do not re-derive it.

Named from decision record 0008 and from the two stack-02 chapters, in `backend/tests/unit/domain/test_patches.py`:

| Test | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `test_apply_empty_is_identity` | A branch with no edits returns the map byte for byte (INV-5) |
| `test_patch_concat_equals_sequential_apply` | Two branches in a row equal the two joined (INV-5) |
| `test_base_graph_unchanged_after_apply` | The base map serializes to the same bytes after the call |
| `test_child_branch_applies_parent_first` | `flatten` puts the parent's edits first |
| `test_apply_rejects_unknown_subject` | An edit naming a claim that is not there returns a violation; never raises, never half-applies |
| `test_retune_changes_only_strength` | One field of one arrow; everything else identical |
| `test_believe_touches_only_user_belief` | `beliefs.model` and `beliefs.market` untouched, everywhere (INV-11) |
| `test_apply_preserves_dag` | After any sequence of edits, the map still has no loops once reflexive arrows are set aside (INV-6) |
| `test_apply_touches_only_the_affected_set` | The *structural* half of locality: every claim outside the affected set is byte-identical in the two **maps** |

`test_intervention_locality` itself — the full statement, over two propagated **worlds** — and `GraphEditMachine` both land in pull request 3, because both need likelihoods and likelihoods do not exist until `propagate` does. The two rules below apply to both.

**The locality tests compute the affected set themselves.** Ten lines against `networkx` inside the test file — ancestors, descendants, over the map the edit leaves behind. It must **not** call `domain.patch.affected_set`, and it must not ask the engine which claims it touched. A test that agrees with the code it is testing is not a test; `interventions.md` says so in as many words.

**They must pin a fully separated claim.** For each of the six operations the test picks at least one claim that is not a descendant of the subject and shares no ancestor with it, and asserts that claim is byte-identical in the two worlds. ## Pull request 3 — `propagate`

```python
def propagate(
    graph: Graph,
    assignments: tuple[Assignment, ...],
    *,
    as_of: date,
    seed: int,
    draws: int = 10_000,
) -> World
```

### The time axis

Day zero is `as_of`. The window runs from day zero to the latest resolve-by date on the map, in whole days. Every date becomes an integer day index at the edge of this function and stays an integer inside it.

**When a claim becomes true.** If an assignment fixes it, on the assignment's `at` day (day zero when `at` is `None`). Otherwise, the earliest day any live incoming arrow reaches it — the day its source became true plus that arrow's `lag`. A claim with neither an assignment nor a live incoming arrow becomes true on day zero: the map carries no timing information about it, and pretending otherwise would be inventing one.

### The arithmetic

At day *t*, for each claim, in an order that always puts causes before effects (topological, reflexive arrows set aside):

```
log-odds(claim, t) = baseline(claim, t) + Σ over live incoming arrows: strength × shape(t − t_source)
```

`shape` is a plain function of elapsed days, zero before it: `impulse` — zero through the lag, then 1, halving every `half_life` day thereafter; `step` — zero through the lag, then 1, held; `ramp` — climbing from 0 to 1 across the lag, then 1, held. A `sustain` arrow's term is zero on any day its source is not true; a `trigger` arrow's term keeps running on its own schedule once fired, whatever the source does afterwards. **That one sentence is the whole domino-and-apple distinction as arithmetic.** Write it in the chapter with the two ASCII pictures `link.md` already draws.

`baseline(claim, t)` is the log-odds of the claim's own `prior` — except while a supposition is holding, when it is ±4.0.

### How a supposition ends — *decided here, and the showcase depends on it*

A supposition (`do`) holds from its `at` day until the first day a live incoming arrow **pushes against the value it supposed** — an arrow that could only have arrived after the `do`, because a `do` cuts the arrows present when it lands. From that day the claim is no longer supposed: its baseline reverts to its own prior and every live arrow decides it. The day it stops is the day the *overriding arrow's source* became true, not the day that arrow's push reaches full size, because that is the day the world changed.

## Pull request 4 — difference, sensitivity, and the two routes

**`diff(world_a, world_b) -> Diff`.** Per claim, one of four states:

| State | When |
|---|---|
| `unchanged` | Present in both and the likelihood moved by less than 0.005 — below what two significant figures can show, so claiming a change would be a lie (NFR-1) |
| `shifted` | Present in both and it moved by 0.005 or more. Carries before, after, and the signed difference |
| `added` | Present in B and not in A |
| `killed` | Present in both, and in B it is either assigned false or no longer has any path from the hypothesis. *Never* "its number got small" — the vocabulary says `killed` means forced false or cut off |

Plus **ranked terminal deltas**: every `market` and `not_tradeable` claim that shifted, ordered by

```
rank = |Δ likelihood| × grounding
grounding = (1 − (hi − lo)) × min(provenance weight of each arrow on the shortest path from the edit's subject to this terminal)
```

with provenance weights `documented` 1.0 · `historical` 0.9 · `market_implied` 0.9 · `argued` 0.6 · `user` 0.6 · `simulated` 0.5 · `asserted` 0.3. This is FR-16's "size of the change and how well-founded it is — the provenance of the arrows behind it and the width of its range, never a self-reported number", made arithmetic. It is *decided here*; the chapter lists it under Open questions.

Plus a **one-line summary** built from a fixed template, never free prose: *"<edit in the user's words> moves <terminal> from <before> to <after> and leaves <n> claims untouched."*

**`sensitivity(world) -> tuple[SensitivityRow, ...]`.** Flip each claim one at a time — a `do` to the opposite of whichever way it more often comes out — re-propagate, and record the signed difference on every terminal. Two thousand draws per flip, not ten thousand, and the row says so. This feeds stack 05's derived stop-loss and stack 06's "spend here" ranking; **no route in this stack**, because nothing on screen reads it yet.

**The routes**, in `backend/src/katalyst/api/worlds.py`, under the `/api/` prefix like everything else:

| Route | Body | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/worlds` | `{base_id, branch, seed, draws?}` — `branch` is a whole `Branch`, sent by the browser, not a stored identifier (there is no store until stack 05) | One `World` |
| `POST /api/worlds/diff` | `{base_id, branch_a, branch_b, seed, draws?}` | One `Diff` |

### The shapes

```python

```python
def apply(
    graph: Graph,
    branch: Branch,
    assignments: tuple[Assignment, ...] = (),
) -> tuple[Graph, tuple[Assignment, ...]] | list[Violation]
```

`apply` folds a branch's edits onto a map, in order, and hands back the map it leaves behind together with every value an edit fixed. It is pure: no clock, no network, no randomness. The optional third argument is what makes law 2 type-check — feed back what a previous `apply` returned and you can apply the next branch on top:

```

```

**What each edit does to the map.** `do`: remove every arrow whose target is this claim **and that is present right now** — a timed assertion, not a seal — and record an assignment. `observe`: remove nothing; record an assignment. `insert`: add the claim and its arrows. `retune`: replace one arrow's `strength` and nothing else. `believe`: write `beliefs.user` on one claim and nothing else, anywhere. `refine`: **not implemented** — return a violation saying it arrives in stack 06.

**Failure is a list of violations, never an exception and never a half-applied branch.** Three new codes join the twelve in `domain/validity.py`, exactly the three `interventions.md` open question 5 proposed: `unknown_target` (the edit names a claim this map does not have), `unknown_link` (it names an arrow this map does not have), `duplicate_id` (an `insert` reuses an identifier). Their messages are interface text — a plain sentence naming the claim or arrow by its words, not by its identifier, like every message already in `validity.py`.

**`flatten`.** A child branch applies its parent's edits first, and `domain/` sees one branch at a time, never the collection. So `flatten(branches: Mapping[BranchId, Branch], branch_id: BranchId) -> tuple[Intervention, ...]` walks the parent chain and concatenates. A parent chain that loops back on itself returns a violation rather than hanging (`branches-and-worlds.md` open question 3, answered here for the walk only — the storage rule is still stack 05's).

**`affected_set(graph, intervention) -> frozenset[PropositionId]`** computes, from the shape of the map alone using `networkx`, the claims an edit is allowed to move. Day zero is `as_of`. The window runs from day zero to the latest resolve-by date on the map, in whole days. Every date becomes an integer day index at the edge of this function and stays an integer inside it.

At day *t*, for each claim, in an order that always puts causes before effects (topological, reflexive arrows set aside):

Research report 02 §3 reports `P(M1)` going from about .61 to about .18 and `P(M2)` from about .54 to about .09. Those are illustrative and the fixture's numbers differ; assert **directions and orderings**, never those values. One warning from the same report: it writes `H → B` as −1.6 because it was thinking about the oil *price*; the fixture writes **+1.6** because `B` is the *claim* "Brent settles below $68", and `link.md`'s rule is that the sign is on the claim. The fixture is right.

---

## Pull request 4 — difference, sensitivity, and the two routes

**`diff(world_a, world_b) -> Diff`.** Per claim, one of four states:

| State | When |
|---|---|
| `unchanged` | Present in both and the likelihood moved by less than 0.005 — below what two significant figures can show, so claiming a change would be a lie (NFR-1) |
| `shifted` | Present in both and it moved by 0.005 or more. Carries before, after, and the signed difference |
| `added` | Present in B and not in A |
| `killed` | Present in both, and in B it is either assigned false or no longer has any path from the hypothesis. *Never* "its number got small" — the vocabulary says `killed` means forced false or cut off |

Plus **ranked terminal deltas**: every `market` and `not_tradeable` claim that shifted, ordered by

```
rank = |Δ likelihood| × grounding
grounding = (1 − (hi − lo)) × min(provenance weight of each arrow on the shortest path from the edit's subject to this terminal)
```

with provenance weights `documented` 1.0 · `historical` 0.9 · `market_implied` 0.9 · `argued` 0.6 · `user` 0.6 · `simulated` 0.5 · `asserted` 0.3. This is FR-16's "size of the change and how well-founded it is — the provenance of the arrows behind it and the width of its range, never a self-reported number", made arithmetic. It is *decided here*; the chapter lists it under Open questions.

Plus a **one-line summary** built from a fixed template, never free prose: *"<edit in the user's words> moves <terminal> from <before> to <after> and leaves <n> claims untouched."*

**`sensitivity(world) -> tuple[SensitivityRow, ...]`.** Flip each claim one at a time — a `do` to the opposite of whichever way it more often comes out — re-propagate, and record the signed difference on every terminal. Two thousand draws per flip, not ten thousand, and the row says so. This feeds stack 05's derived stop-loss and stack 06's "spend here" ranking; **no route in this stack**, because nothing on screen reads it yet.

**The routes**, in `backend/src/katalyst/api/worlds.py`, under the `/api/` prefix like everything else:

| Route | Body | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/worlds` | `{base_id, branch, seed, draws?}` — `branch` is a whole `Branch`, sent by the browser, not a stored identifier (there is no store until stack 05) | One `World` |
| `POST /api/worlds/diff` | `{base_id, branch_a, branch_b, seed, draws?}` | One `Diff` |

`engine/worlds.py` sits between the route and `domain/`: it finds the base map in `fixtures.catalogue`, resolves the parent chain with `flatten`, reads `as_of` from the stored example's `fixture_date`, mints identifiers, and passes a seed through. It is the only place any of that happens, because `domain/` reads no clock and knows no store.

A rejected edit comes back as **422 with the list of violations**, each with its code, its subject and its plain sentence — the same shape a rejected proposal already has. Never a 500, never a silent repair.

Then: run `make types`, read the generated `frontend/src/api/schema.ts` end to end, and fix the pydantic side if a union reads badly. Never hand-patch the generated file. Finally mark `ARCHITECTURE.md` §3 (the flow of a generation — steps 4 and 7 are now real) and §5 (where each invariant is enforced) with what is true.

---

## Pre-decisions — settle nothing twice

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding two-dimensional Monte Carlo simulation for second-order uncertainty and variability separation in risk assessment:

## Overview

A two-dimensional (second-order) Monte-Carlo simulation is a simulation where the distributions reflecting variability and uncertainty are sampled separately in the Monte-Carlo simulation framework, so that variability and uncertainty in the output may be estimated separately.

## Key Contributors

A two-dimensional (or second-order) Monte Carlo simulation was proposed to estimate the uncertainty in the risk estimates arising from parameter uncertainty (Cullen and Frey, 1999). Additionally, the need to separate uncertainty and variability in risk assessments has been increasingly emphasized (Hoffman and Hammonds, 1994, Frey and Rhodes, 1996, Rai and Krewski, 1998, Nauta, 2000, Mitchell and Csillag, 2001), with Vose (2000) also contributing foundational concepts.

## Importance of Separation

The separation of uncertainty and variability allows us to identify the steps that can be taken to reduce the total uncertainty, to gauge the value of information or of potential system changes, and to avoid the serious errors induced by mixing variables with parameters.

## Applications

In recent years, the second-order Monte Carlo simulation (MCS), also known as two-phase or two-dimensional MCS, has been extensively used in various risk assessment domains, particularly in microbial and food safety risk assessment.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Sobol sensitivity indices estimators:

## Overview of Sobol Indices Estimation

Sobol indices are Monte Carlo estimated using a standard estimator, and sensitivity analysis can be conducted directly from the Monte Carlo sample at hand (i.e., the one generated to assess model output uncertainty) or can require extra Monte Carlo simulations by following an appropriate sampling design.

## Different Estimation Approaches

Several Monte Carlo estimators exist for computing Sobol indices:

1. **Standard Sobol Method**: This method allows the estimation of the indices of the variance decomposition, sometimes referred to as functional ANOVA decomposition, up to a given order, at a total cost of (N + 1) * n where N is the number of indices to estimate.

2. **Saltelli Estimators (sobol2002)**: These implement Monte Carlo estimation of Sobol' indices for both first-order and total indices at the same time (altogether 2p indices), at a total cost of (p+2) × n model evaluations.

3. **Jansen Estimators**: These implement Monte Carlo estimation of Sobol' indices for both first-order and total indices at the same time (altogether 2p indices), at a total cost of (p+2) × n model evaluations.

4. **Martinez Estimators**: These implement Monte Carlo estimation of Sobol' indices for both first-order and total indices using correlation coefficients-based formulas, at a total cost of (p+2) × n model evaluations.

## Regression-Based Approaches

The search results include references to Gaussian process regression frameworks for estimating Sobol indices from existing data, though detailed information about specific "given data" regression estimators is limited in these results.

"""A belief: a likelihood with an honest range and a name on it.

A bare number on a box is a claim from nowhere. A belief is a likelihood that
says whose it is and how sure it is: a value between 0 and 1, a range around it,
and an owner — the model, the user, or a market. Every claim on the map carries
up to three of them side by side, and they are never combined into one.

That is the product in one design choice. The model's .61, the market's .48 and
your own .30 on the same claim are not three attempts at one true number to be
averaged away. They are the disagreement you are about to trade: model minus
market is the edge, user minus model is the argument you are having with the
tool.

Both classes here are frozen — once built, an instance cannot be changed. A
change is a new instance, recorded as an intervention on a branch.
"""

from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, model_validator


class Belief(BaseModel):
    """A likelihood with an honest range and a name on it.

    `p` is the likelihood, `lo` and `hi` are the range around it, and `owner`
    says whose number this is. There are exactly three owners and no code path
    ever combines two of them into one number.

    A belief is a number, never text. This layer does not round it and does not
    store it as a string; rounding happens once, at the moment of display.
    """

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    # Open question 1 in spec/graph/belief.md: a belief records no provenance,
    # so a model number anchored on a documented count and one asserted from
    # nothing look alike. Owner is not yet the whole answer.
    p: float = Field(
        ge=0.0,
        le=1.0,
        description=(
            "How likely the claim is to come out true, from 0 (certainly not) to 1 (certainly yes)."
        ),
    )
    lo: float = Field(
        ge=0.0,
        le=1.0,
        description="The bottom of the honest range around `p`. Never above `p`.",
    )
    hi: float = Field(
        ge=0.0,
        le=1.0,
        description="The top of the honest range around `p`. Never below `p`.",
    )
    owner: Literal["model", "user", "market"] = Field(
        description=(
            "Whose number this is: the model's estimate, the user's own, or a live "
            "price at a venue."
        ),
    )

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def _range_is_ordered(self) -> "Belief":
        """Check that low is at most the likelihood, which is at most high.

        The field bounds above already cover 0 and 1; this covers the order.

        Returns:
            This same belief, once the order has been checked.

        Raises:
            ValueError: If the three numbers are not in order.
        """
        if not (self.lo <= self.p <= self.hi):
            raise ValueError(
                "a belief must satisfy low <= likelihood <= high; got "
                f"low={self.lo}, likelihood={self.p}, high={self.hi}"
            )
        return self


class Beliefs(BaseModel):
    """The three voices on one claim: the model's, the user's, and a market's.

    Three named slots, deliberately not a dictionary, so that nothing can loop
    over them and average them by accident. `model` is always present. `user` is
    absent until the user says what they think. `market` is absent when no venue
    quotes this claim — and absent means the words "no market", never a blank and
    never a stand-in number.

    The field named `model` is legal. Pydantic protects names beginning with
    `model_`, so `model_config` and `model_dump` are reserved; plain `model` is
    not one of them. It stays `model` because that is the word the shared
    vocabulary uses, on the canvas and in the code alike.
    """

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    model: Belief = Field(
        description=(
            "What the model thinks, with this claim's causes taken into account. Always present."
        ),
    )
    user: Belief | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description=(
            "What the user thinks. Written only by the `believe` intervention. None means "
            "the user has not said."
        ),
    )
    market: Belief | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description=(
            "What a venue is currently pricing, read live and read-only. None means no "
            "venue quotes this claim."
        ),
    )

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def _owners_match_slots(self) -> "Beliefs":
        """Check that each slot holds a belief owned by the voice the slot is named for.

        A belief sitting in the wrong slot would make the never-merge rule
        unenforceable: a user's number could sit in the model's chip and nothing
        would notice.

        Returns:
            This same set of beliefs, once every slot has been checked.

        Raises:
            ValueError: If any slot holds a belief owned by someone else.
        """
        for slot, belief in (("model", self.model), ("user", self.user), ("market", self.market)):
            if belief is not None and belief.owner != slot:
                raise ValueError(f"the '{slot}' slot holds a belief owned by '{belief.owner}'")
        return self

I've performed a web search on the logit-normal distribution with emphasis on elicitation, quantiles, median, log-odds scale, and subjective probability uncertainty. Here are the key findings:

## Logit-Normal Distribution Overview

The logit-normal distribution involves the standard logistic function and the inverse cumulative distribution function of a normal distribution. The logistic normal distribution is a generalization of the logit–normal distribution to D-dimensional probability vectors by taking a logistic transformation of a multivariate normal distribution.

## Elicitation and Quantiles

The search results show that quantile-based approaches are commonly used for elicitation of uncertainty distributions. Experts can be elicited for three quantiles: the median, a quantile above the median and a quantile below the median, typically the 5% and 95% quantiles.

## Log-Odds Scale in Probability

Log odds is argued to be a fundamental representation of frequency/probability used by the human brain, and the LLO transformation in various areas reflects a common mechanism to deal with uncertainty. Subjective frequency/probability in a wide variety of tasks can be fitted by the LLO function with two parameters, and on log odds scales the LLO function is a straight line with slope and crossover point.

## Fitting Distributions to Subjective Probability

An iterative approach can be used to encode elicited probabilities as probability distributions, first attempting to fit a flexible metalog distribution, then a Johnson Quantile-Parameterised Distribution, a three-component skew-normal mixture model, and finally a shifted log-normal distribution.

You are doing a literature survey for a design decision. Search the web (WebSearch/WebFetch). Do NOT write any files. Return findings directly as your final message, terse and dense, with working URLs.

Topic: non-sampling alternatives for propagating *epistemic* (second-order) uncertainty through a small causal graph of binary propositions where influences add on the log-odds scale.

Cover, each with 3-8 lines and citations (paper/book + a stable URL):
1. **Subjective logic (Audun Jøsang)** — opinion triple (belief, disbelief, uncertainty) + base rate, the bijective mapping to a Beta distribution, what "uncertainty mass u" means, the deduction/abduction (conditional) operators and the fusion operators. Key: does subjective logic give a principled "wider = less sure" and can it chain through a graph? What are its known limitations (operator non-associativity, dependence/correlation handling, the "uncertainty explosion" or loss of information along chains)? Cite Jøsang's book "Subjective Logic: A Formalism for Reasoning Under Uncertainty" (Springer 2016) and any survey/critique.
2. **Credal networks / imprecise probability** — Levi, Walley's imprecise Dirichlet model, credal network inference complexity (NP-hard even for polytrees? cite Cozman, de Campos, Maua). What is 2U / the exact algorithms for binary polytrees?
3. **Probability bounds analysis / p-boxes** — Ferson & Kreinovich, the RAMAS / "Constructing probability boxes and Dempster-Shafer structures" Sandia report SAND2002-4015; Williamson & Downs' probability arithmetic. Known critique: bounds become vacuous quickly when dependence is unknown (Fréchet bounds).
4. **Delta method / first-order error propagation** — propagating a variance through a nonlinear function; specifically, if X ~ Normal(mu, sigma^2) on the logit scale and p = sigmoid(X), what are the standard approximations for E[p] and Var[p]? Cite the classic "probit approximation" / MacKay's logistic-Gaussian integral approximation E[sigmoid(X)] ≈ sigmoid(mu / sqrt(1 + pi^2 sigma^2 / 8)) — find the original source (MacKay 1992 "The Evidence Framework Applied to Classification Networks", or Bishop PRML §4.5.2) and state the exact formula and its accuracy. Also the simpler kappa = 1/sqrt(1 + pi sigma^2/8) variant. State clearly which constant is correct.
5. Anything on **Dempster-Shafer / Transferable Belief Model** being overkill for small models, briefly.

Be honest about which of these are overkill for a 60-node prototype and which are elegant. Give me exact formulas where they exist.

toolUseResult.prompt:
You are doing a literature survey for a design decision. Search the web (WebSearch/WebFetch). Do NOT write any files. Return findings directly as your final message, terse and dense, with working URLs.

Topic: non-sampling alternatives for propagating *epistemic* (second-order) uncertainty through a small causal graph of binary propositions where influences add on the log-odds scale.

Cover, each with 3-8 lines and citations (paper/book + a stable URL):
1. **Subjective logic (Audun Jøsang)** — opinion triple (belief, disbelief, uncertainty) + base rate, the bijective mapping to a Beta distribution, what "uncertainty mass u" means, the deduction/abduction (conditional) operators and the fusion operators. Key: does subjective logic give a principled "wider = less sure" and can it chain through a graph? What are its known limitations (operator non-associativity, dependence/correlation handling, the "uncertainty explosion" or loss of information along chains)? Cite Jøsang's book "Subjective Logic: A Formalism for Reasoning Under Uncertainty" (Springer 2016) and any survey/critique.
2. **Credal networks / imprecise probability** — Levi, Walley's imprecise Dirichlet model, credal network inference complexity (NP-hard even for polytrees? cite Cozman, de Campos, Maua). What is 2U / the exact algorithms for binary polytrees?
3. **Probability bounds analysis / p-boxes** — Ferson & Kreinovich, the RAMAS / "Constructing probability boxes and Dempster-Shafer structures" Sandia report SAND2002-4015; Williamson & Downs' probability arithmetic. Known critique: bounds become vacuous quickly when dependence is unknown (Fréchet bounds).
4. **Delta method / first-order error propagation** — propagating a variance through a nonlinear function; specifically, if X ~ Normal(mu, sigma^2) on the logit scale and p = sigmoid(X), what are the standard approximations for E[p] and Var[p]? Cite the classic "probit approximation" / MacKay's logistic-Gaussian integral approximation E[sigmoid(X)] ≈ sigmoid(mu / sqrt(1 + pi^2 sigma^2 / 8)) — find the original source (MacKay 1992 "The Evidence Framework Applied to Classification Networks", or Bishop PRML §4.5.2) and state the exact formula and its accuracy. Also the simpler kappa = 1/sqrt(1 + pi sigma^2/8) variant. State clearly which constant is correct.
5. Anything on **Dempster-Shafer / Transferable Belief Model** being overkill for small models, briefly.

Be honest about which of these are overkill for a 60-node prototype and which are elegant. Give me exact formulas where they exist.

input.prompt:
You are doing a literature survey for a design decision. Search the web (WebSearch/WebFetch). Do NOT write any files. Return findings directly as your final message, terse and dense, with working URLs and dates.

Topic: **are LLM-stated probability intervals / confidence ranges meaningful?** And: is *ensembling N independent LLM runs* a better empirical source of spread than asking the model to state a range?

Cover, each with 3-8 lines + citation URL:
1. **LLM forecasting calibration** — Halawi et al. 2024 "Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models" (arXiv 2402.18563 / NeurIPS 2024): what did they find about calibration, and did they use ensembling/aggregation of multiple runs? What was the effect of averaging multiple forecasts?
2. **AIA Forecaster (2025)** and any 2025-2026 work on LLM forecaster systems reaching superforecaster parity — find it, name the org, summarise the aggregation method (e.g. multiple independent forecasts + aggregation/extremization).
3. **Paleka et al. — consistency checks for LLM forecasters** ("Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters", ICLR 2025?): what incoherence do they find (e.g. violations of probability axioms across logically related questions)? This matters because it says whether a model's *stated* spread can be trusted.
4. **Verbalised confidence / verbalized uncertainty** — work showing LLMs' stated confidence intervals are overconfident/too narrow. E.g. Lin, Hilton, Evans "Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words" (2022); Xiong et al. "Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?" (ICLR 2024); Tian et al. 2023 "Just Ask for Calibration"; any paper on eliciting *intervals* (numeric ranges) from LLMs and measuring their empirical coverage (e.g. "LLMs are overconfident interval estimators", conformal prediction for LLM numeric answers). Find concrete coverage numbers if any exist (e.g. "stated 90% intervals contain the truth only X% of the time").
5. **Sampling-based / self-consistency uncertainty** — evidence that the *spread across independent samples at temperature* is better calibrated than *stated* confidence. Semantic entropy (Farquhar et al., Nature 2024), self-consistency, "sample-and-measure-disagreement" approaches.
6. Anything on **eliciting Beta distribution parameters or quantiles directly from an LLM**.

Give concrete numbers and dates where available, and say plainly which findings are robust and which are single-paper.
